stem: A 22-year-old man notices pale, finely scaling patches on his chest and back that failed to tan over the summer. The areas are oily, with no redness or itch. A potassium hydroxide preparation of the scale shows short hyphae mixed with round yeast forms.
oneliner: 22M + pale, finely scaly patches on chest and back that did not tan + KOH short hyphae and round yeast → which skin layer holds the organism?
ask: In which skin layer does this organism live?

whyNot.B: The organism is shed with **scale** on the surface; the basal layer holds dividing keratinocytes and melanocytes, and **KOH on scale** would not find hyphae there
whyNot.C: The scale itself contained the organism; **dermal invasion** would give deep inflammation, not a **non-inflamed superficial scale**
whyNot.D: Deep dermal infection would cause **nodules or abscesses**; his skin shows **fine scale only**
whyNot.E: Deep follicle infection suggests **folliculitis or tinea capitis**; his lesions are **flat scaly patches**, and the yeast sits in the scale

why: The organism, **Malassezia**, feeds on skin lipids and stays in the **keratin layer**, so it shows up as **short hyphae and round yeast ('spaghetti and meatballs')** in a KOH scraping. Because it never invades living epidermis, there is **little inflammation**; the patches stay pale because the azelaic acid it makes **inhibits melanin production** in the skin below.

idea.rule: Superficial mycoses stay in the stratum corneum and cause scale, not inflammation.
also: Tinea nigra (Hortaea werneckii) is a painless brown superficial patch on the palm
Piedra is a superficial mycosis of the hair shaft
Tinea versicolor responds to topical selenium sulfide or azoles because the fungus sits at the surface
